_readme: Answers for the Ask Isaac chat on the tennis page. Each topic has an id, 'covers' (what questions it answers — this is what Jev reads to pick it), the answer shown to the visitor, and optional buttons. 'answer_parent' (optional) is shown instead when the visitor is asking for their child. 'next' is up to three follow-up questions shown as tappable chips after the answer; phrase them as a visitor would. Button types: book (private | semi | hitting), email (subject), link (href), scroll (#section), open (a popup's id, e.g. clinicList or giftForm). A tip topic's 'title' is its heading on the practice tips page (/tips/), which the build makes from these answers. 'misuse' is what the chat says to abuse or attempts to give it instructions; 'personal' is prefixed when someone types contact details. Edit freely; keep every fact true to the page. If nothing fits a question, the chat shows 'fallback'. After editing, run node tools/i18n/build.mjs and update the translated answers it lists.
greeting: Hi! These are my answers to what people ask most. Try prices, where I coach, who I teach, booking, or something in your game you want to fix.
fallback: I don't have that written down here. Email me and I'll answer you directly.
unavailable: The chat isn't answering right now. Email me and I'll get back to you.
misuse: I can only answer questions about lessons here.
personal: Please leave out phone numbers, addresses, schools and full names here. Email me for anything personal.

topics.covers: A greeting or small talk with no real question, such as hi, hello, hey, or asking whether anyone is there.
topics.answer: Hi! Ask me about lessons, prices, where I coach, or how to book.

topics.covers: The visitor says thank you, goodbye, or that they have what they need.
topics.answer: Anytime. Hope to see you on court.

topics.covers: How much lessons or sessions cost, rates, pricing, fees, or comparing prices.
topics.answer: Private lessons are $80 an hour, or 5 for $375 and 10 for $700. Semi-private is $110 an hour for two players, so $55 each. A hitting partner session is $45 an hour. Adult clinics are priced per group, so the cost per player falls the more of you there are.

topics.covers: Lesson packages, buying several lessons at once, bulk prices, discounts or deals.
topics.answer: For private lessons: 5 for $375 or 10 for $700, paid in person. That's $75 and $70 an hour instead of $80.
next: What if I need to cancel?

topics.covers: Buying lessons as a gift, gift cards or gift certificates, or giving tennis lessons to someone as a present.
topics.answer: Yes. You can give one private lesson ($80), 5 private lessons ($375), 10 private lessons ($700) or a hitting session ($45). Send me the request, we settle payment in person, and I'll give you a printable gift card.

topics.covers: What a private (one-on-one) lesson is, what it covers, or who it is for.
topics.answer: A private lesson is one-on-one, $80 an hour, for juniors and adults, tailored to your level. We work on stroke and serve mechanics, footwork and court movement, the slower, softer balls younger players learn on, match-readiness for tournaments, and you leave with a practice plan for between sessions.

topics.covers: Semi-private lessons: two players sharing a lesson, bringing a friend, sibling or partner, doubles lessons for two, or being matched with a partner.
topics.answer: Semi-private is two players of a similar level on one court, sharing the hour and the cost: $110 for the hour, $55 each. Same stroke and serve work as a private, plus live rallies and points against each other, and doubles positioning if that's what you're training for. Each player still gets individual feedback. Bring your own partner, or ask me to match you with one.
next: Can you find me a partner?
How much is a private lesson?

topics.covers: Hitting partner sessions: someone to rally, practise or play sets with, without coaching or instruction.
topics.answer: A hitting session is hitting, not coaching — $45 an hour, 60 minutes or longer. I feed and rally at your level so you get reps: cross-court and down-the-line rallies, serve and return practice with a live returner, and tie-breaks or sets on request.

topics.covers: Adult clinics, group lessons, joining a group, or lessons for three or more people together.
topics.answer: Adult clinics are small groups on a single court: drills and live-ball games with enough rotation that nobody stands around, working on rally tolerance and consistency under pressure. They're priced per group. Join the clinic list with your level and the times that suit you, and I'll put you in a group with players like you, or bring your own group.

topics.covers: The visitor asks which lesson or option they should choose, or describes themselves and wants a recommendation.
topics.answer: Quick guide: one player who wants coaching — a private lesson. Two of you at a similar level — semi-private. You just want someone reliable to hit with, no instruction — a hitting session. Three or more — an adult clinic. The box under the lesson cards can also match you from a sentence.

topics.covers: Where lessons happen, the address or courts, or whether Isaac can travel to the visitor's home, club, school or another court.
topics.answer: Lessons are at my home court: the Toscana Apartments tennis courts in Irvine. Players come to me — I can't travel to other courts, clubs or homes.

topics.covers: Who Isaac teaches: ages, levels, kids, juniors, adults, complete beginners, or advanced players.
topics.answer: Juniors from complete beginners up (the youngest start on a slower, softer ball, so first-timers are welcome) and adults at any level. Most of my work is with developing juniors, and I run adult clinics for players who want more consistency and a clearer plan once points start.
topics.answer_parent: Kids from complete beginners up. The youngest start on slower, softer balls (red, then orange, then green) and move up as they're ready, so a first-timer is welcome. I'm approved under USTA Safe Play, background-checked and SafeSport-trained, and RSPA-certified.

topics.covers: Isaac's certifications or qualifications (RSPA, USPTA, PTR), whether he is certified, background checks, SafeSport, or whether he is safe to coach children.
topics.answer: I'm certified by the RSPA, the Racket Sports Professionals Association (formerly the USPTA), and approved under USTA Safe Play: background-checked and SafeSport-trained. I've coached since 2023.
next: How long have you been coaching?

topics.covers: How to book or schedule a lesson, sign up, or reserve a time.
topics.answer: Hit any Book button on this page and pick a time on the calendar. Booking online just holds the time — no card, no deposit. When you book, tell me your level and what you're working on, and I'll come with a plan.
topics.answer_parent: Pick a time on the calendar and book in your own name. In the notes, tell me your child's age, how long they've played and what they'd like to work on, and I'll plan the first lesson around them. No card, no deposit: you pay in person.
next: What if I need to cancel?

topics.covers: When Isaac is available: days, times, weekends, evenings, how often, or how soon a lesson can happen.
topics.answer: Coaching is a part-time job for me, fitted around school, so my schedule stays small. The booking calendar shows every open time. If nothing there works, email me when you're free and I'll reply with availability.

topics.covers: How or when to pay, payment methods, deposits, or whether a card is needed to book.
topics.answer: You pay in person. Booking online holds the time — no card, no deposit.

topics.covers: Cancelling, rescheduling or moving a lesson, the cancellation policy, being sick or running late, or what happens if it rains or is too hot.
topics.answer: Cancel or move a lesson with 24 hours' notice; later cancellations are charged. If rain or heat cancels a lesson, we reschedule at no cost.

topics.covers: What to bring, whether the player needs their own racket or equipment, or borrowing a racket.
topics.answer: No racket yet? You can borrow one of mine.

topics.covers: What the first lesson is like, what to expect, or how to prepare for it.
topics.answer: When you book, tell me your level and what you're working on, and I'll come to the first session with a plan built around it.
topics.answer_parent: Tell me your child's age and level when you book, and I'll come with a plan built around them. Young beginners start on a slower, softer ball.

topics.covers: How long lessons or sessions last.
topics.answer: Lessons are 60 minutes. Hitting sessions run 60 minutes or longer.

topics.covers: Isaac's coaching experience, how long he has coached, where he coached before, or his playing history.
topics.answer: I've been coaching since 2023. I started as a Junior Pro at LifeSport Libertyville, then joined the Pro Staff of Grip N Rip, the junior program at Newport Beach Tennis Club. I'm RSPA-certified, and I played four years of high school varsity.

topics.covers: Isaac's coaching style, philosophy, or how he teaches.
topics.answer: Fundamentals first, then everything else. Getting the basics right early means progress keeps compounding, and almost every player improves faster than they expect once the practice is deliberate. You leave each lesson with a practice plan for between sessions.

topics.answer: Private lessons include match-readiness for tournament play, and in a hitting session we can play tie-breaks and sets on request.

topics.covers: The visitor wants a tip or advice on improving their tennis, or asks what they should work on, without describing a specific problem yet.
topics.answer: Tell me what's going wrong, like "my serve goes into the net" or "I can't keep a rally going", and I'll give you one thing to try. These are quick fixes; in a lesson we'd find the real cause.
next: My serve goes into the net
I can't keep a rally going

topics.title: My serve goes into the net
topics.covers: The visitor's serve keeps going into the net, or their serve is too low.
topics.answer: A serve in the net usually means the toss is too low or too far in front, so you hit down on the ball too early. Toss a little higher, just in front of your hitting shoulder, and reach up to hit it at full stretch. Practise ten tosses without swinging: each one should come down in the same spot, in front of your front foot.
next: How can I practise on my own?

topics.title: My serve goes long
topics.covers: The visitor's serve goes long, past the service line, or out.
topics.answer: A long serve usually comes from a toss drifting behind you, which opens the racket face at contact. Keep the toss slightly in front, hit up and over the ball, and let the racket turn over after contact. Aim for the middle of the box, not the lines.
next: My serve goes into the net

topics.title: I double fault a lot
topics.covers: The visitor double faults a lot, their second serve is weak or unreliable, or they get nervous on second serves.
topics.answer: Most double faults come from hitting the second serve like a slower first serve. A second serve needs more spin, not less speed: brush up the back of the ball so it clears the net with room and dips into the box. Practise a basket of second serves only, and count how many land in.
next: My serve goes into the net

topics.title: My forehand goes into the net
topics.covers: The visitor's forehand goes into the net, or their groundstrokes are too low.
topics.answer: Forehands into the net usually mean the swing is too flat or the contact is late. Start the racket below the ball and finish high over your opposite shoulder, and meet the ball out in front of your body. Aim about three feet above the net: that height is your margin.
next: I'm always late to the ball
I can't keep a rally going

topics.title: My forehand flies long
topics.covers: The visitor's forehand flies long, sails out the back, or has no control.
topics.answer: A forehand that sails long is usually hit flat with an open racket face. Brush up the back of the ball for topspin, so it dips down into the court, and finish the swing over your shoulder instead of straight at the target. Aim deep to the middle, a few feet inside the baseline.
next: My forehand goes into the net

topics.title: My backhand is weak
topics.covers: The visitor's backhand is weak or inconsistent, or they avoid hitting backhands.
topics.answer: A weak backhand usually starts with a late turn. As soon as you see the ball coming to that side, turn your shoulders so your back is partly to the net, then swing from low to high out in front. Rally backhand to backhand cross-court with a partner until it feels routine.
next: I'm always late to the ball
I can't keep a rally going

topics.title: I can't keep a rally going
topics.covers: The visitor can't keep a rally going, makes too many unforced errors, or wants more consistency.
topics.answer: Rallies end early when every shot aims too close to the lines or the net. Aim higher over the net and deep to the middle of the court, and count your rallies: try to beat your own record, not your partner. Consistency comes before power.
next: My forehand goes into the net
How can I practise on my own?

topics.title: I'm always late to the ball
topics.covers: The visitor is late to the ball, feels rushed or jammed, or wants better footwork or movement.
topics.answer: Being late is usually a footwork problem, not a swing problem. Do a small split-step just as your opponent hits, so you're on your toes when you read the ball, then take small adjusting steps before you swing. Shadow it at home: split, turn, swing, recover.
next: I can't keep a rally going

topics.title: I'm uneasy at the net
topics.covers: Volleys, net play, overheads, or the visitor is nervous or uncomfortable at the net.
topics.answer: At the net, less is more: no big backswing. Keep the racket up in front of you, turn your shoulders, and punch the ball with a short motion, stepping forward as you hit. Start close to the net with a partner feeding gently, then move back.
next: Can two of us share a lesson?

topics.title: I play worse in matches
topics.covers: The visitor plays worse in matches than in practice, gets nervous, or wants match strategy.
topics.answer: Most players tighten up because they try harder shots under pressure. Pick a simple plan before the match, like deep cross-court until you get a short ball, and use the same short routine between every point. Practise with a score, too: games and tie-breaks, not just rallies.

topics.title: How can I practise on my own?
topics.covers: How to practise alone or between lessons, drills to do at home, or practising against a wall.
topics.answer: A wall is the best practice partner there is: rally forehands and backhands against it, aiming above a line. A basket of serves on an empty court builds a reliable toss, and shadow swings in front of a mirror fix technique without a ball. Short and often beats long and rare.
next: My serve goes into the net
I can't keep a rally going

topics.title: My elbow hurts (tennis elbow)
topics.covers: The visitor's elbow or forearm hurts when they play, or they ask about tennis elbow: what causes it, how to avoid it, or how to get rid of it.
topics.answer: Tennis elbow is a sore spot on the outside of the elbow, where the muscles that lift the wrist attach to the bone. On court it usually comes from a late, wristy backhand: the ball meets the racket beside you instead of in front, the wrist bends, and the forearm takes a jolt it isn't built for. Meet the ball out in front with a firm wrist and let the shoulders do the swinging, loosen your grip, and try softer strings or a bigger grip. Rest it while it's sore, and if it still hurts after a couple of weeks, see a doctor.
next: Do I need my own racket?

topics.title: How can my child practise at home?
topics.covers: A parent asks how their child can practise at home, get started, or stay interested in tennis.
topics.answer: Keep it short and playful: catching and throwing, bouncing a ball on the racket, rallying over a line on the driveway with a soft ball. A few minutes several times a week builds more than one long session. In lessons, young beginners use slower, softer balls, so they rally sooner.
